read.where: Split the taps into **core** handles (the beers that sell every week) and **rotating** handles (seasonal, local, a brewery you’re featuring). Cover the **flavor families** the Brewers Association uses: **Clean & Crisp**, **Malty & Sweet**, **Fruity & Spicy**, **Sour & Funky**, **Hoppy & Bitter**, **Dark & Roasty**, so two handles don’t do the same job. Plan the hardware too: the Draught Beer Quality Manual warns that **cider, root beer and flavored beers** can permanently taint a line, and **nitro** beer needs its own **gas blend** and **restrictor faucet**.

stops.name: Hardware
stops.text: Cider and nitro on **their own lines**.

read.mixup: A long list isn’t a good list. Two IPAs that taste alike take a handle from a beer that would sell.
read.sayIt: Tonight’s rotating tap is new: crisp and light, if you like a pilsner.

video.title: Beer distributors lose profit on expired kegs

keyPoints.line: on tap and flavor may change.

read.bigIdea: A keg should empty before it fades.
read.where: The Draught Beer Quality Manual says beer in kegs on tap **longer than 45 days** may no longer taste as the brewer intended, and each brewer has its own **freshness window**. So size the keg to the sales: **days on tap = pints in the keg ÷ pints sold a day**. A half barrel holds about **124 pints**, a quarter about **62**, a sixtel about **41**. A beer selling **3 pints a day** takes about **41 days** to empty a half barrel, right at the limit, but only about **14 days** for a sixtel.

stops.name: Sales
stops.text: Pints sold **a day**, from the POS.

read.mixup: A half barrel isn’t always cheaper. If it sits past its freshness window, the last third is waste.

video.title: Behind the Scenes: The Making of a Beverage Calendar

read.where: Some styles carry their season in their name. The BJCP says **Helles Bock** is also called **Maibock**, a seasonal beer tied to **spring** and the month of **May**. **Märzen** (“March beer”) was brewed in **March** and lagered over the summer; it was the amber lager served at **Oktoberfest** from **1872 to 1990**, when the golden **Festbier** took over. **Winter Seasonal Beers** suggest cold weather and the **Christmas holiday**: stronger, darker and often **spiced**. Plan rotators a season ahead, with the distributor’s release dates.
read.mixup: Märzen and Festbier aren’t the same beer. Märzen is amber; Festbier is golden, and has been the festival beer since 1990.

keyPoints.line: one wholesaler per brand, per area.

read.where: In Michigan, beer moves through **three tiers**: the **brewer** sells to a licensed **wholesaler** (the distributor), and the wholesaler sells to **retailers** like us. A brewer gives a wholesaler the rights to its brands in a **sales territory**, so a brand usually comes from **one** distributor in our area. The exception: a Michigan **micro brewer** that sells no more than **2,000 barrels** a year may deliver to retailers itself, but not in a territory where it has given a wholesaler **exclusive rights**.
read.mixup: You can’t shop a brand around to the cheapest distributor: in our area it usually comes from the one wholesaler that holds its rights.

unverified: How many handles are core and how many rotate is house practice: the GM sets our split.

Michigan self-distribution: the 2,000-barrel limit and the exclusive-territory rule come from the Liquor Control Commission’s self-distribution page and summaries of MCL 436.1203a (2020); the statute text itself wasn’t read.
That a brand usually comes from one wholesaler in an area reflects Michigan’s exclusive beer sales territories (the franchise sections of the Liquor Control Code, not read for this lesson).
Keg pint counts are nominal (no foam, no loss); real yield is lower (Lesson 5).
